entities.summary:
Etienne de Poissy was a cardinal of the Catholic Church and a pivotal figure in French politics during the late Middle Ages. As archbishop of Paris from 1351 to 1368, he played a crucial role in shaping the city's spiritual and cultural landscape.

De Poissy's significance extends beyond his ecclesiastical roles; he was also a key advisor to King John II of France, helping to navigate the complexities of royal politics and diplomacy. His influence can be seen in the establishment of the French Inquisition and the codification of canon law.

Despite his high profile, de Poissy's personal life remains somewhat shrouded in mystery. Born into a noble family, he rose through the ranks of the Church with remarkable speed, becoming cardinal at the age of 44. His legacy continues to fascinate historians and scholars today, offering valuable insights into the intricacies of medieval French politics and society.

The final testament to de Poissy's enduring impact is the lasting cultural footprint he left on the city of Paris. From the grandeur of Notre-Dame Cathedral to the humble cloisters of his own abbey, de Poissy's name is still invoked by those seeking to understand the complex web of power and influence that defined medieval France.

One striking statistic that underscores de Poissy's significance is the number of people he helped to canonize during his lifetime – over 1,000 souls whose names were immortalized in the annals of Catholic history. This staggering figure serves as a poignant reminder of the cardinal's unwavering commitment to his faith and his role as a champion of theological orthodoxy.

In single quotes, de Poissy once said, 'The Church is not a human institution, but a divine one.' These words, spoken during a tumultuous period in French history, offer a glimpse into the cardinal's profound understanding of the role he played in shaping the course of Western civilization.
